title: The bow tap at Lark Court
public_context: Small chamber groups rehearse in halls where stage crews coordinate program changes and lighting. The following fictional document is a stage manager's record from a recital in a modest hall. It concerns an evening of chamber music and the kinds of cue notes a house crew may keep.
source_title: Lark Court stage manager's cue ledger for the Thursday recital
source_text:
The Thursday recital at Lark Court opened with the Lantern Trio: Mina Vale on clarinet, Oren Pell on viola, and Jo Ren at the piano. Its second piece, Three Rooms, alternates a long clarinet tone with a low piano figure before returning to the opening refrain. The house manager's cue ledger was written for the ushers and stage crew, who needed to know when the lamps could be raised between pieces.

At the afternoon rehearsal, the trio reached the page turn between the long tone and the refrain. Jo's left hand had to leave the keyboard to turn two sheets, and the clarinet's entrance depended on hearing a soft viola harmonic from the stage's far side. The turn caught once; Oren waited, then the players restarted the passage from the previous bar. The manager made a pencil mark beside the page and asked the trio to run the transition again.

Before doors opened, Oren proposed a short bow tap during the written rest. Jo would repeat the two-bar bass figure while Mina held her place; on the second tap, Mina would enter at the printed refrain. The trio tried it three times from different distances and kept the same order of notes. Oren asked the stage manager to move the music stand slightly inward so all three could see his hand. The ledger calls this a cue for the performers, not a signal to the lighting booth.

During the concert, the page caught at the same turn. Jo continued the two-bar figure twice, Oren gave the bow tap, and Mina entered at the refrain without a restart. The three players watched one another. The house log notes that no lamp changed during the passage and the audience did not interrupt. The next piece began after the regular applause, when the stage manager raised the aisle lights.

After the set, the manager removed the stand clip and tucked it in the drawer with the ledger. A penciled note beside the cue reads, “leave the old pencil mark until the printed part is reset.” The performance copy went back to Jo's folder; Oren kept the annotated rehearsal page. There was no amplifier at Lark Court. For this cue, the players relied on sight and timing.

At the bottom of the record the manager listed the lamp change for the next piece and the crew call for the following morning. No seating survey was filed. The surviving sheets do not carry a date for the next time the trio would use Three Rooms, and the rehearsal page's pencil note has no initial beside it.

consistency_questions.question: How did the rehearsal problem and the concert cue fit together?
consistency_questions.reference_answer: The page turn caught in rehearsal and led to a restart; the trio then planned a repeated piano figure and bow-tap entry. At the concert the same page turn caught, but the cue brought Mina in at the refrain without a restart.

consistency_questions.question: What distinguishes the performers' cue from the house lighting sequence?
consistency_questions.reference_answer: Oren's tap was arranged for the players during the passage. No lamp changed then; the stage manager raised the aisle lights after applause as the next piece began.
